summary: At 69 people per square mile spread across 606 square miles of Sierra Nevada foothill country, Amador County has roughly the population density of a national forest with a few towns tucked into it — and that's not far from the literal truth, since the county's eastern half climbs into the Eldorado National Forest above 5,000 feet. The western stretches roll through oak-studded grasslands and old Gold Rush corridors, with Jackson and Sutter Creek serving as the tiny commercial spines where most shopping, dining, and government jobs concentrate. A home-price-to-income ratio around 5.2 is genuinely moderate by California standards, and the $1,380 median rent sits well below what you'd find even an hour downhill in Sacramento — but the tradeoff is a thin local job market anchored heavily by county government, healthcare at Sutter Amador Hospital, two tribal casinos, and a state prison, meaning many residents commute 45-plus minutes west on Highway 88 or 16. Summers are classically foothill-hot with generous sunshine — 9.3 hours daily on average — while winters bring real cold at higher elevations and occasional snow. The 95.6% graduation rate across its 19 schools is notably high, though standardized math scores lag significantly below state benchmarks. Amador is a place where affordable California homeownership and genuine mountain-adjacent wildness coexist with geographic isolation and a very short list of local employers.
